title: Setting a Summer Reading Project
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: This post argues for treating professional reading as a bounded project organised around a framework rather than as general self-improvement, and then demonstrates the method on Stuart's own summer. He contrasts two modes: an earlier year spent on the full exploration of a single book, Schmoker's Focus, from which he says much of his later thinking grew, and the current year spent finalising a literature base for a book of his own. The substance is a reading list sorted by the components of his Non-Freaked Out Framework, which is what makes it a method rather than a list. Under noncognitive factors he prefers Farrington's free critical literature review to any book, arguing it is more coherent and usable than the character-strengths material he previously wrote about. Under knowledge he separates how the brain works, Oakley, Make It Stick, Willingham, from why knowledge matters and how to build knowledge-rich curricula, where he treats Hirsch as the must-read. The closing principle is the transferable one: reading time is finite, so choose the books most likely to produce the fruit you are after.
points: The organising idea is that professional reading should be run as a bounded project against a framework, which supplies the criterion for what to leave unread.
Two legitimate modes are contrasted, a year spent fully exploring a single book versus a year assembling a literature base for a specific piece of work.

The noncognitive recommendation is pointed: Farrington's free critical literature review is preferred to any book, and explicitly to the character-strengths framing Stuart himself used to write about.
Knowledge is split into two distinct reading tasks, how the brain works and why knowledge matters for curriculum design, with different authors serving each.
The closing constraint is the useful one for any teacher: you will only read so many books in a lifetime, so select for the fruit you are actually after.
quotes: In my last post, I suggested that there's a time to take on no new reading at all, instead setting one's course for the full exploration of a single book.
The best book on this topic isn't a book, it's a critical literature review.
This provides a masterful overview of how noncognitive factors work together; it's much more coherent and usable than the character strengths I used to write about all the time.
Then, we need to understand why knowledge matters (to literacy, to thinking, to knowing more) and how we might go about creating knowledge-rich curricula.
If you've been around a while, you know my thoughts on argument: it's not central enough to American schooling, despite its centrality to a life of the mind.
Remember that, in all of our reading, we strive to be purposeful. You'll only get to read so many books in your lifetime, so choose the ones most likely to produce the fruit you're after.
